[B][u]The Road to Revolution - 1885 to 1929[/u][/b]

The House of Bahman had ruled for almost 90 years, from 1840 to 1929, having replaced their parent house, the House of Kadivar, which ruled before them from 1747 to 1840. The last Shah, Jalaludin Shah, began his rule from the age of 15 in 1885 following the early death of his father, Nadir Shah, to illness.

He ruled as a modernising figure. He introduced a constitution that limited his role in government to the appointment of the Ministers, the veto of laws, and as supreme commander of the armed forces. His constitution also created the first parliament of Dhornaper, the Majlis, with a limited form of democracy that allowed land owning males to vote. His vision for democracy was still too new and the majority of eligible voters never voted. His modernisation drive also brought him to accept international aid through friendly ties with neighbouring states that had formed or occupied parts of the historical core territories of Dhornaper such as ULR.

His cousin, Ayub Khan, was twelve years his senior and had been the Shah's opposite in many ways. Ayub Khan began his political career as an officer in the military at the age of 20 and was rapidly promoted to a general owing to his royal blood. In 1895, he successfully put down a tribal revolt against the Shah's taxation policies in Afghanistan Sharghi. His military successes rose him to national prominence and he became the Shah's Prime Minister five years later. As Prime Minister, he showcased his personality and regularly acted in ways that displeased the Shah. Where Jalaludin Shah had been a softer and more diplomatic figure, Ayub Khan had been an aggressive and forceful character. His tenure was turbulent: on numerous occasions, the Shah had to block his much more aggressive pushes for modernisation and his irredentist foreign affairs attitude which had left Dhornaper internationally isolated and economically stagnant.

Eventually, the backlash from international governments and the economic situation left Ayub Khan in a precarious position. His irredentist and aggressive attitude had become too much to bear. Ayub Khan tendered his resignation in 1920. To the shock of many including Ayub Khan himself, Jalaludin Shah accepted his resignation. The Shah went further and introduced a constitutional amendment that forbade any member of the royal family from being a Minister and consolidated his position to free himself of Ayub Khan's influence.

For the time being, Ayub Khan was forced into the background of national politics but he still wielded enormous influence, especially amongst the armed forces which adored him. Ayub Khan nursed his beliefs, reflected on his tenure, and maintained his prominence in the armed forces, helped by his status as a general on the retiree list and as a national hero. His contacts with his former subordinates were maintained. He was biding his time to return.

[b]Valddera Statement on Regional Threats in Toqastan[/b]

Valddera reiterates its steadfast support for Toqastan and its sovereign right to govern its own affairs. Recent attempts by certain powers to portray themselves as all-seeing, all-knowing observers in the region reveal more about their insecurity than their strength. Publicly flaunting surveillance capabilities and issuing warnings from afar may impress those unfamiliar with real influence, but in practice, such gestures are little more than noise.

We are well aware of the resources and positions of those who seek to intimidate. While they may boast of advanced technology, stealth platforms, or high-end weaponry, true operational effectiveness comes not from flashy displays, but from strategic coordination, understanding, and the ability to act decisively when the time comes. It is worth noting that overconfidence and reliance on empty posturing often leave the most belligerent actors exposed, vulnerable to the consequences of their own miscalculations.

Valdderas support for Toqastan is neither symbolic nor superficial. It is grounded in practical measures, long-term planning, and unwavering commitment to regional stability. Any attempts to interfere with Toqastan, its allies, or the logistical and humanitarian support provided by Valddera will be met with resolute and calculated responses. We do not make idle threats, our actions are measured, precise, and backed by resources and expertise unmatched by those who prefer spectacle over substance.

To those who rely on fear, intimidation, or hollow demonstrations of strength: consider carefully the gap between rhetoric and reality. While one can spend time showcasing capabilities, another ensures those capabilities are matched by strategy, discipline, and the willingness to act effectively. Empty posturing may garner headlines, but it does little to influence the actual balance of power.

Valddera will continue to engage constructively with Toqastan, strengthen its regional position, and ensure that any efforts to destabilise the area are met not with panic, but with deliberate and decisive measures. The Belorev region will not be dictated to by those who mistake noise for authority. Those who attempt to intimidate must understand that their performance is observed, and evaluated, not merely celebrated.
